sources.shell: Walls about 5 cm thick, as the Dufuna canoe's (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dufuna_canoe). Carved from one log, a side stands from the bottom with its gunwale free, and a breaker bends it as a cantilever: by the model, 8.4 voxels from the bottom's edge to the gunwale
sources.depthMetres: Keel to gunwale: a 0.21 m draft with one paddler and a hand's breadth or two of side above it, which a full bilge brings down to the water
sources.waterplaneSquareMetres: A 4.5 m log, 0.75 m wide, with rounded ends: about two thirds of its box, so that 450 L aboard settles her by her 0.2 m of side

sources.charMillimetresPerHour: A burn of 3 to 5 hours chars 6 to 13 mm of wood (Agency House dugout diary, 2021-2023, agencyhouse.org/dugout-canoe)
sources.hollowings: Wet clay goes along the rim before each fire (PHMC dugout project, 2005; SUNY Potsdam, 2015), and the fire is tended round the clock until the clay is spent, about a day and a night: 7 cm at a time, the 0.42 m hollow takes six fires and about a week, as Wampanoag builders burn a mishoon for 6 to 10 days (Plimoth Patuxet, The Making of a Mishoon)
sources.hollowDepthMetres: Rim to floor of the hollow: the 0.5 m hull less its 7.5 cm bottom
sources.clay: Wet clay one voxel thick over the rim outline the shape draws (its Clay group), at vanilla's 25 voxels a ball (BEClayForm.PutClay)
sources.axeEdgeMetres: Char has lost its fibres and crumbles, so a stroke breaks it away down to the sound wood along its whole sweep across the hollow, a strip as wide as the axe's edge, about 10 cm on a felling axe
sources.hollowBeamMetres: The hollow's width the stroke sweeps: the hull's 0.75 m beam less its two 7.5 cm walls (bin/lib/hulls/dugout.py)
sources.wallMetres: Her shell's 5 cm walls: a fire burning with the rim unguarded chars it at the hollow's rate, and once the char reaches through a wall's thickness the blank is spoiled
sources.secondsPerStroke: The best working rhythm with an axe is 25 to 35 strokes a minute (H. Glaser, physiology of forestry work, FAO)
sources.hewSaturation: As hard as a patch of mending: hewing out a day's char by hand

sources.pushNewtons: A sustained two-handed push by an adult, about 300 N (Snook and Ciriello, 1991, maximum acceptable forces)
sources.friction: Wood sliding over wet sand or mud, about 0.4

sources.bowOnDrag: A fine bow parts the water with next to no pressure drag at a paddler's speeds: her drag ahead is the friction on her wetted surface
sources.broadsideDrag: A hull's side across the flow: a round bottom and its mirror in the surface make a cylinder of her length to twice her draft, which takes about 1.0 (Hoerner 1965, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, ch. 3: 1.2 across a subcritical flow, 0.82 of it for a cylinder ten times as long as it is thick)

sources.heave: Balance: 400 kg of log rises slowly to a crest; a light hull rises with it, a heavy one lets it climb the side
sources.capsizeBreakerMetres: Seamanship: a breaking wave as high as an open boat's beam can roll it over
sources.rollResponse: A round-bottomed log has little form stability: tippy in a sea
sources.pitchResponse: A long, heavy log rides through the swell with little pitch

sources.capacityLitres: The hollow of a 5 m log, about 0.5 m wide and 0.35 m deep, half of its box
sources.deckSquareMetres: Its open hollow, 5 m by 0.6 m, catches the rain
sources.drainLitresPerHour: One log, no seams: nothing leaks
